previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of stroke, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, diabetes, and recurrent infections was admitted for a clogged GJ tube, urinary tract infection, and tracheostomy leak. He developed hypoxia during transport due to a mucus plug, which resolved with suctioning. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics—cefepime and daptomycin—due to a history of resistant organisms, despite contaminated urine culture. The tracheostomy was successfully exchanged, and the GJ tube was unclogged using a 5 cc syringe and diet coke. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. His infection resolved, leg pain was managed with increased gabapentin, fentanyl patch, and capsaicin cream, and he was discharged to extended care with follow-up plans for INR monitoring and CK checks.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,
It was a pleasure caring for you during your admission for foley 
catheter replacement. The staff at your nursing home were unable 
to replace your foley catheter, so you were brought to the ED 
where the urologists were able to successfuly replace the 
catheter. In the ED a urine test was suggestive of a urinary 
tract infection, and your white blood cell count, a marker of 
infection, was elevated. You received a dose of antibiotics in 
the ED, but your white blood cell count came down to normal 
range the following morning, so it was felt you most likely do 
not have an infection, so you will be able to return to the 
nursing home without antibiotics.
